I see that this sub is a bit sparse compared to the other hellhole and has considerably fewer subscribers. Thus, I feel we may not have the same critical mass of expertise to where certain fundamental ideas are covered as frequently.

I've also had a lot of real life experiences recently with rich, highly educated adults who don't seem to know shit from shinola about investing and it's horrifying, so I wanted to write a brief guide for everybody's sake.

Let me throw out a few concepts for new investors:

* Understand the differences between investing and speculation. Investing is putting your money where some kind of return is almost assured. Good examples of this: buying shares in a viable business and taking dividend payments, being a lender and charging interest that is legally enforceable. Speculation is buying something on the theory that it *might* increase in value so you can turn around and sell it later. That is not investment. 99% of "investors" are just speculating with the stock of publicly traded companies.

* There are many other investments in the world besides stocks. One way to learn about some of them is to check out PortfolioVisualizer.com, click "backtest asset allocation," then note the LONG list of different types of investments. Look all of them up on Wiki or Investopedia and see what they are. This is not a comprehensive list.

* There are individual stocks, then there are index funds and other exchange traded funds (ETFs). ETF prices move with some kind of weighted average of hundreds of individual stocks, thus diversifying your portfolio and lowering your risk. Before attempting to pick individual stocks it may be wise to understand the [efficient market hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficient-market_hypothesis). Summarized, there are thousands and thousands of highly trained, experienced professionals, analysts and investors using mountains of information 24/7 to try to determine what the exact price of any given company's stock ought to be and trading it accordingly. There are billions of dollars riding on this industry. While you *might* know something they don't know about a specific company, the odds are against you. Therefore, it is commonly advised to stay away from individual stocks unless you are unapologetically gambling.

* [Modern portfolio theory,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory) I strongly suggest you look into it. To summarize, the more different types of investment you hold at once, the lower your risk of losing money overall because if one asset goes down, another may go up to compensate. A classic example of this is the not quite inverse relationship between stocks and bonds: investing some in stocks and some in bonds will lower your risk compared to investing in either alone. This is the same general idea behind favoring index funds over picking individual stocks. This is more specific than screeching "don't put your eggs in one basket!" like a broken record, because plenty of people hear that and think that rather than having 100% of their money in Apple, it means they should also buy some Google and Starbucks because they have tunnel vision and think stocks are the only investments on earth. For that reason I am more specific.

* Understand the concept of dollar cost averaging. Look it up. To summarize, if every month you put exactly $500 into some index fund, you will often do better than if you bought in all at once at the end of the year. This is because the fund's price changes, yet your cash input does not: if the fund's value is $250 in January, you buy 2 shares, but if in February the fund's value drops to $10, you buy 50 shares. This exaggerated example should demonstrate how the practice of dollar cost averaging "automatically times the market," you automatically buy more shares when the price is low and buy fewer shares when the price is high. This is a particularly relevant concept for those of us working for a living who may not have a huge wad saved up to invest.

* Understand the concept of rebalancing your portfolio. Some people rebalance their investments once a year or on some other schedule, others rebalance when a certain portion of their portfolio gets too large or too small measured as a percentage of the whole portfolio. I'd advise you to read on your own time why this is good, run the math yourself and play with some backtesting tools like I linked above to figure out how this helps you.
